events.label: Korean War
events.occurrence: US considers nuclear attacks on North Korea and Manchuria

occ.source: President Truman, news conference, 30 Nov 1950 (American Presidency Project transcript)
occ.quote: There has always been active consideration of its use. I don't want to see it used.

nm.source: President Truman, news conference, 30 Nov 1950 (American Presidency Project transcript)
nm.quote: There has always been active consideration of its use. I don't want to see it used.

events.note: Public record of consideration of atomic use dates from this press conference; the specific plans for strikes on North Korea/Manchuria (e.g. military requests, later FRUS releases) were disclosed later and were not searched. Earliest found, not proven earliest.

events.label: First Indochina War
events.occurrence: US considers tactical nuclear use at Dien Bien Phu
events.note: Not resolved. Internal deliberations (Radford 7 Apr 1954 NSC; Eisenhower 30 Apr 1954 'we might give them a few') are only documented via later sources (Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists 2016 article gives dates but not first public disclosure). Candidate earliest public accounts not verified: Chalmers Roberts's 1954 press account, Bidault's claim, Eisenhower's memoir 'Mandate for Change' (1963, pp. 354-355, cited in FRUS 1952-54 vol. XIII pt 2 doc 820 editorial note). Not confirmed to mention atomic use.

events.label: Suez Crisis Coincidence
events.occurrence: NORAD receives four coincident reports (aircraft over Turkey, MiGs over Syria, bomber down, Soviet fleet) during Suez
events.note: Not resolved. Individual reports (Syria MiGs, Turkey overflights, Canberra shot down) were circulating in Nov 1956 (a CNA study reproduces such rumours), but I found no dated source that links them as four coincident NORAD reports; only later retrospectives (Canadian Pugwash 20 Mishaps list, GlobalSecurity), which cite Sagan 1993. Not verified.

events.label: U.S. accidental bomb drop in New Mexico
events.occurrence: B-36 drops bomb south of Albuquerque

occ.source: Associated Press (via Los Angeles Times), 'Accident Revealed After 29 Years: H-Bomb Fell Near Albuquerque in 1957', reporting Albuquerque Journal FOIA story
occ.quote: Newly released government documents reveal that a 42,000-pound hydrogen bomb ... accidentally fell from a bomber near Albuquerque 29 years ago

nm.source: Same AP/Los Angeles Times article
nm.quote: But it didn't go off, and we don't know how serious the accident was.

events.note: Headline says revealed after 29 years, but the blast was felt locally in 1957 and a local 1957 newspaper report could exist; I could not check 1957 archives. Weapon was unarmed (no capsule), so the 'near detonation' sense is weak; B is the same article.

events.label: U.S. accidental bomb drop in Savannah, Georgia
events.occurrence: B-47 drops bomb near Savannah

occ.source: Military announcement that search for the bomb was unsuccessful (as stated in Wikipedia, 'Tybee Island mid-air collision')
occ.quote: On April 16, the military announced the search had been unsuccessful.

nm.source: 1966 JCAE testimony (W.J. Howard) describing a complete weapon with a capsule, released 1994, per Center for Arms Control fact sheet
nm.quote: 1966 Congressional testimony were released in 1994 and revealed the weapon was indeed a complete, fully-functional bomb with a plutonium pit.

events.note: Wikipedia says AP stories on 5-6 Feb 1958 covered the collision but does not say they mentioned the bomb; whether the loss was public in Feb 1958 is unresolved (A may be Feb 1958). Wikipedia page itself is a secondary. The capsule claim is disputed by SAC documents.

events.label: Second Taiwan Strait Crisis

nm.quote: the United States came fairly close to using tactical nuclear weapons

events.note: A (the shelling, Aug 1958) was certainly in 1958 newspapers but I did not fetch a dated source, so null. B: this is the first public release of Halperin's classified analysis found; CNN (2021) notes it was already public that Eisenhower debated nuclear use, so earlier public statements (Eisenhower memoir, 1960s scholarship) likely exist and were not searched.

events.label: A Nuclear Attack? Or the Moon?

events.note: Not resolved. Secret IDA study (1975) and NSA release are later archival; Hart-Goldwater 1980 report (govinfo CPRT-96SPRT68531O) concentrates on 1980 alerts and I did not confirm that it mentions 1960. Retrospective papers cite it (Univ. Waterloo paper, 1980s, citing Hart-Goldwater and Ford, The Button, New Yorker, 1 and 8 Apr 1985). No 1960s press source found.

B: Wikipedia says Ralph Lapp gave an early (erroneous) account in 1962; I did not verify whether it described near-detonation, so an earlier B may exist. events.label: British Alerts

nm.quote: Both the Thor missile force and V-bombers were at fifteen minutes readiness.

events.label: U2 Flights into Soviet Airspace
events.occurrence: U-2 strays over Chukotka on a polar route; MiGs scramble; nuclear-armed F-102As escort it to Alaska

occ.checked_against: a full-text copy, not linked (see raw-manifest.json for its hash)
occ.check: not checked: page fetched, quote not found

events.note: Occurrence: Khrushchev's private letter of 28 Oct 1962 complained of the Chukotka overflight (Kennedy replied with regret; both letters in FRUS XI, also printed in Documents on Disarmament 1962 vol. II), but the date of first public release was not established. Garthoff cites Hilsman 1967 for the Kennedy quip; Hilsman page not seen, so 1967 is inferred from the citation (low). Sagan 1993 says the incident 'was well known'. Near-miss: Garthoff (1987/1989) already notes the escorting F-102s carried nuclear missiles, which pre-dates Sagan 1993, contradicting the National Security Archive 2022 page statement that Sagan was the first to report it (quote there: 'Political scientist Scott Sagan was the first to report (in 1993)', https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/cuba-cuban-missile-crisis/2022-10-27/cuban-missile-crisis-60-most-dangerous-day). Whether the footnote is in the 1987 first edition is unconfirmed (1989 ed. seen). Dobbs 2008 says the full story was still classified.

events.label: Operation Anadyr (B-59)

nm.source: Alexander Mozgovoy, Komsomolskaya Pravda (1995), as described by the National Security Archive
nm.quote: about the near-use of a nuclear-tipped torpedo by the captain of B-59

events.note: Exact 1995 date and title of the Komsomolskaya Pravda article not found. Arkhipov's own Moscow talk (14 Oct 1997) responded to it. Wide Western knowledge came in 2002: Mozgovoi's book (spring 2002), Havana conference (Oct 2002), National Security Archive briefing book 75 (2002-10-31) and its 'The Submarines of October' page. Orlov's account is disputed; other commanders doubt Savitsky would have ordered it. Earliest found, not proven earliest.

nm.quote: Captain Nikolai Shumkov ordered the preparations of torpedoes, including the tube holding the nuclear torpedo

events.label: U2 Spy Plane Shot Down Over Cuba

occ.quote: On October 31, Acting United Nations Secretary-General U Thant returned from a visit with Premier Fidel Castro and announced that Anderson was dead.

nm.quote: if the first one [is shot down], we have to take it out [the offending SAM site], and then announce what's happened.

Near-miss: the 23 Oct decision to retaliate for a shootdown is shown in the ExComm tapes; I could not confirm the publication year of the transcript (1997 book is an inference) and Robert Kennedy's Thirteen Days (1969) or earlier memoirs may state it sooner (not checked). Wikipedia says Ellsberg heard in 1964 from R. Kennedy that a second shootdown would trigger retaliation, privately.

clocknote: Asteroid passages: median 1 day late. Nuclear close calls with a checked date: median 24 years, middle half 2.1–30.2 years. Hover a bar for the close calls in it.
findings: The keeper is the state, and the clock is its archive. Of the 53 close calls the four keepers list between 1945 and 1998, this work could date and check 34: the earliest public source it found that says how near each came. The median wait is 24 years (middle half 2.1 to 30.2). 23 waited ten years or more; 8 were known as close calls within a year: Korean War (1950, within the year); U.S. strategic bomber crash in Spain (1966, within the year); DPRK shootdown of U.S. EWAC aircraft (1969, within the year); Sino-Soviet conflict (1969, within the year); Soviet Missile Headed Toward US? (1980, within the year); Failed coup (1991, 10 days); Gulf War: Israeli nuclear weapons (1991, within the year); Russian False Alarm (1995, within the year).

Reported is not counted. Many were news at once: a crash, a lost bomb, a false alert. Of the checked rows, 8 were reported as events within a year of happening (where an occurrence date could be checked). What waited was the sentence that turns an event into a near miss: that a switch held, that a captain was talked down, that an officer judged an alarm false.

Most of the Cold War's close calls are heard after it ended. 18 of the 34 reached the public record as close calls in 1992 or later. Play the clock: by the end of 1977, 6 of them were known; the rest arrive after. The longest waits: U.S. mistaken order during Cuban Missile Crisis (1962, 53 years); Vietnam War (Fracture Jaw) (1968, 51 years); Confusing Solar Flares and Nuclear Attacks (1967, 50 years).

One reader opened 9 of them. 9 of the 34 checked close calls are first described as close calls in one book: Scott Sagan's The Limits of Safety (1993), written from wing histories and command-post logs he obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. They are the cluster of red points in 1993. A political scientist's requests, not the events, set their date.

Who decides that it counts. In the asteroid record a formula decides and a telescope sets the delay. Here three hands act in turn: whoever keeps the file decides when it is opened; whoever first writes it up (a senator's report, a memoir, a declassified memo, a journalist) decides that it was near; and the keepers, starting with Phillips in 1998, decide which of these make the list. A close call that is still closed is not late. It is not yet anything.
method: Events: the Field's study 7 (Who keeps the close calls, 2026-10-10), 53 events coded from four keepers' lists (Phillips 1998, Chatham House 2014, Future of Life Institute 2016, Wikipedia as served 2026-10-10), read at a pinned commit by build_data.py. The date an event happened is the earliest date any keeper gives for it.

Two dates per event, found by web research: reported as an event, the earliest dated public source that the occurrence happened at all; known as a close call, the earliest dated public source that says how near it came, in the sense the keepers' description gives. Each date carries its source, a link, and a quotation of at most 25 words.

Every quotation was checked by verify_sources.py: the linked page was fetched and the quotation looked for in its text. Only a close-call date whose quotation was found counts; the others stay in the table in grey with the reason (no source found, page refused, quotation not on the page). An occurrence date that could not be checked is replaced by the close-call date, so the middle rail is a floor.

A date given only as a year or a month is placed at the start of that period: a line is never drawn longer than its evidence. A found quotation proves that the page says it, not that no earlier source exists. Earlier sources would shorten lines; none would lengthen them.
Some sources are secondary: an encyclopedia or an archive's summary that states when the first account appeared. The table names the source as found.

Nothing here estimates how near any event came; that is the keepers' judgment and the sources'. Asteroid delays are from AFTER IT PASSED (JPL close-approach and small-body data): passage to first observation, for the passages first seen afterwards.
Evidence beside the page: research.json (the dated sources), verification.json, raw-manifest.json (SHA-256 of each fetched page; pages not committed), data.json, verify_browser.mjs.
siblings: The Field, Who keeps the close calls (study 7): four keepers agree on 3 of 53 events. This work takes the Field's 53 events as its material and asks the question the Field did not: not which keeper lists an event, but when any public record could first have listed it. Every keeper wrote after the clock had already run.

The Field, How far the record sees (study 8): the asteroid record's reach sets its denominator. The nuclear record's denominator is set by what is still closed, and no plot of the open part can show its edge.

The Atelier, The Hinge and Near to What: the keeper who writes the hinge decides how near; in the asteroid record the passage rewrites what it was near to. Here the hinge itself arrives late: the sentence that something could have gone otherwise is often the last part of the record to be written.
